case_study_insert.main_stem: Montagu Cork Flooring Co-operative (MCFC) is a cooperative in the eco-materials and construction-materials sector, laminating cork-bark granules into floating floor tiles and acoustic underlay for low-energy housing. Founded in 2016 by 21 members led by general manager Rosa Inglis, it employs a workforce of 29 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic, member-elected leadership. MCFC plans to invest $480,000 in an automated lamination and edge-sealing press, financed by a $280,000 bank loan and a $200,000 community share issue. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. Its offcut dust contamination rate has reached 5.8%, wasting premium cork and slowing lines.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research and Production Summary — October 2025: MCFC laminated and edge-sealed 11,250 units last quarter; 5.8% of tiles failed adhesion and thickness testing, up from 3.6% a year ago; customer complaints fell from 16 to 10 per month. Average order fulfilment is 5 days. Market research of 340 eco-home builders and homeowners found that 64% would pay a 7% premium for certified renewable-bark flooring, and 59% rank fast, reliable supply as decisive. A maintenance log shows the press stopped 8 times last quarter; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $700 per employee, while on-the-job training lacks certification, and 7 of 29 staff lack lamination-press lockout certification.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, its third rise this year, increasing variable-rate loan costs. (2) Cork bark, natural resin and freight input costs rose 10.6% year-on-year, and construction-input inflation stands at 6.1%. (3) The national minimum wage will rise by 3.0% to $11.80 per hour from April 2026, and government home retrofit grants for low-energy housing grew by $1,200.

questions.question_text: MCFC plans to finance part of its lamination and edge-sealing press with a community share issue. Explain two advantages for MCFC of using a community share issue to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A community share issue spreads ownership across the 21 founding members and local supporters instead of concentrating risk with one lender, which fits the co-operative constitution and means the $200,000 raised typically carries no fixed repayment schedule or collateral call on the press itself. With the base rate raised to 5.25%, every variable-rate dollar of the alternative $280,000 bank loan adds interest MCFC cannot pass on easily; community shares instead carry flexible, patient capital that members understand and rarely rush.

Point 2: Member investors are customers too — likely builders, homeowners and housing co-ops — so the issue strengthens the local market for certified renewable-bark flooring exactly where the 64% of surveyed buyers willing to pay a 7% premium live. They campaign for MCFC, recommend it in community groups, and stay patient on returns. It also avoids the bank's covenants over the flat democratic structure, preserving member control of pressing schedules, hires and the eco-housing tender pipeline rather than subordinating the co-op to lender conditions.

Quality of finance: Using a $200,000 community issue for part of the $480,000 package means the bank loan covers only $280,000, keeping annual repayments within cash flow at 45,000 units of output and matched against the 7% premium opportunity.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Montagu Cork Flooring Co-operative and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: MCFC is launching its certified renewable-bark flooring for low-energy housing. Consider eco-home exhibitions, social media influencer marketing, or sponsorship of a DIY home improvement programme. Which should MCFC choose to promote the flooring? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Eco-home exhibitions: Standing at regional eco-home and green-building shows lets MCFC put physical cork tiles in buyers' hands, demonstrate the renewable-bark chain of custody, and capture the 340 eco-home builders and homeowners who are its exact segment. The 64% who would pay a 7% premium can touch and compare laminated samples, and the co-op can sign builders on the day. Drawbacks: exhibition slots, travel and sample freight cost real money, only a handful of shows run each year, and MCFC still needs follow-up conversion to orders.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with renovation and eco-living influencers puts renewable-bark flooring in front of younger, design-led homeowners at low cost per view, with trackable links and code-driven orders. Drawbacks: credibility is uneven — influencers cannot credibly certify adhesion results or fire performance — green claims among influencers are increasingly distrusted, and algorithm changes can wipe reach overnight; it will not convince volume housebuilders or councils specifying low-energy housing.

Sponsorship of a DIY home improvement programme: A regional TV or streaming sponsorship gets MCFC's logo and renewable story into thousands of homes weekly and suits big visual stories. Drawbacks: cost is disproportionate to a 29-person co-operative financing an automated press, audiences are broad and low-intent, and attribution is weak — the 59% who rank fast reliable supply as decisive will not wait for a DIY episode to emerge as buyers.

Recommendation: MCFC should choose eco-home exhibitions, supported by a small influencer seeding budget for the highest-energy shows. Exhibitions convert the exact technical buyers identified in its research into specifiers and orders, which no media spend can match for credibility; influencers alone cannot certify quality, and DIY programme sponsorship is unaffordable and untrackable. Exhibitions reject the spray-gun approach to marketing in favour of measurable, trust-based selling — the right model while the $480,000 press beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MCFC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MCFC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why influencers and programme sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: MCFC's offcut dust contamination rate has reached 5.8%. Explain two benefits for MCFC of using democratic, member-elected leadership to improve quality in its pressing team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic, member-elected leadership gives MCFC's 29 workers a genuine voice in setting pressing schedules, dust-extraction routines and lockout rotas around the lamination line. Feeling ownership of the process satisfies esteem and social needs (Maslow), lifts commitment, and directly attacks the 5.8% contamination rate: members who help design dust controls stop the line earlier and suggest cheaper capture improvements — smaller granule bins, extraction hood repositioning, moisture testing of incoming bark — protecting the 11,250 units laminated last quarter and the thin margins behind them.

Point 2: Member involvement raises the quality of everyday decisions — moisture checks on bark deliveries, granule sifting, edge-sealing inspection — without a supervisor layer the co-op cannot afford. Higher trust also cuts the overtime and absenteeism that follow autocratic overwork on a noisy pressing floor, helping MCFC keep the 5 days fulfilment promise valued by the 59% of builders in the research, reduces costly rework of failed edge seals, and reinforces the member culture that underpins the community share issue's credibility with lenders and heritage builders alike. Workers consulted this way also police each other's technique, which is exactly what a 5.8% contamination rate needs most.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MCFC's contamination rate, workforce and output.

questions.question_text: Seven of MCFC's 29 staff lack lamination-press lockout certification. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at $700 per employee. Which should MCFC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training the 7 staff at the press teaches MCFC's own granule grading, dust extraction and edge-sealing settings, costs nothing in course fees, keeps the 11,250 units laminated last quarter moving, and lets senior members mentor lockout practice machine-by-machine — precisely the machine whose 8 stoppages stretched dispatch and whose faults drive the 5.8% contamination rate. Drawbacks: mentor time comes from pressing output, bad habits pass operator to operator, and the training lacks external certification — a serious gap when press incidents follow those stoppages and insurers increasingly demand accredited lockout logs and documented competencies for every operator who touches the line.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $700 per employee gives structured, accredited lockout/tagout certification covering energy isolation, bolster-plate safety, guarding and emergency response, costing $4,900 in total — affordable against the $480,000 press and less than one hour of bark-sealing rework each month. Drawbacks: 7 of 29 operators leave for a day or two during the busiest fulfilment period, the syllabus is generic to standard presses rather than MCFC's bark-lamination settings, and travel plus backfill erodes margin exactly when the 5 days promise is already under pressure.

Decision: MCFC should choose on-the-job training with an external assessor signing off each operator. It preserves scarce pressing hours, tailors learning to the exact faults driving 5.8% contamination, and closes the certification gap at a fraction of the $4,900 fee. Full off-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because nobody else can fit MCFC's granule lines to a standard syllabus, and losing a quarter of the press team during the ramp-up risks the 59% delivery promise after 8 press stoppages have already stretched dispatch beyond the 5 days standard. The external assessor keeps insurers satisfied while the knowledge stays where the faults actually occur — on the pressing floor, not in a classroom generic to every lamination plant in the region.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MCFC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of MCFC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of MCFC with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MCFC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($15.00 − $9.00) = $180,000 ÷ $6.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.00 − $9.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MCFC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. MCFC's managers can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 45,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 15,000 units and giving confidence to commission the automated press without over-ordering stock.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.00 lets managers model the 7% certified renewable-bark premium the 64% of surveyed buyers support; a price of $16.05 would lift contribution to $7.05 and fund quality assurance on the dust controls.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $180,000 and contribution per unit lets managers test whether the $280,000 bank loan can be serviced alongside member withdrawals, by forecasting contribution earned above the 30,000-unit breakeven each month.
4. Unit cost data ($180,000 ÷ 45,000 units + $9.00 = $13.00 a unit) lets managers benchmark each quarter, attack the 5.8% contamination rate driving rework, and renegotiate the $9.00 variable cost toward cork bark, resin and freight amid the 10.6% input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 15,000 units at 45,000 units output; 7% premium-pricing modelling at $16.05; $280,000 loan-service feasibility alongside member withdrawals; and unit-cost benchmarking at $13.00 to attack the 5.8% contamination rate amid 10.6% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MCFC's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MCFC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 34.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 36.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.5%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $2,750,000 to $3,150,000 while cost of sales grew only from $1,815,000 to $2,016,000, so the trading surplus widened to $935,000 and then $1,134,000. Operating profit moved from $275,000 on sales of $2,750,000 to $378,000 on sales of $3,150,000. Capital employed grew from $2,200,000 to $2,520,000 as the press project was funded, and interest payable rose from $90,000 to $105,000.

Evaluation: Performance strengthened on every measure. The share of revenue kept after production costs widened from 34.0% to 36.0%, reflecting better bark selection, less dust contamination and the certified renewable label commanding the 7% premium accepted by 64% of surveyed buyers. The surplus after operating costs improved from $275,000 to $378,000, and the return earned on the enlarged capital base rose from 12.5% to 15.0%, so the new press is already out-earning its funding cost. Caution is warranted: capital employed grew by $320,000, the 5.8% contamination rate still destroys margin, and interest payable rose to $105,000 alongside the $280,000 loan — so fuel-freight inflation of 10.6% could squeeze the gain quickly if unaddressed.

Conclusion: MCFC's financial position has improved. Both trading margins and the return on capital employed moved favourably, rooted in genuine waste reduction and premium certification rather than accounting effects. The co-op should commission the new press, keep pressing dust controls tight to push past 10.0% to 12.0%, and lock freight and bark contracts before the next inflation print.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on whether MCFC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MCFC of switching to cork bark sourced solely from certified renewable plantations.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified renewable-bark sourcing lets MCFC market flooring that stores carbon for its entire service life, cutting embodied carbon per unit and winning specifications in low-energy housing projects — exactly the segment the 64% of surveyed buyers willing to pay a 7% premium, and the government's $1,200 home-retrofit grant, now incentivise. It also secures bark supply against harvest stoppages in Portugal and Spain, protects the 5 days fulfilment promise the 59% of builders rank as decisive, and differentiates MCFC from concrete-based flooring suppliers in local authority tender documents that now score recycled-content and carbon scores explicitly.

Disadvantage: Certified bark carries a price premium and longer supplier qualification cycles — plantation audits, chain-of-custody paperwork and minimum-rest-harvest rules — pushing up the $9.00 variable cost just as cork-bark and freight inputs rose 10.6% year-on-year. Certification audits also add admin cost for a 29-member flat co-op, and any failed audit — for example, a supplier harvesting too aggressively in a cork oak stand — would suspend the certification MCFC's marketing depends on overnight, jeopardising the eco-home contracts that justified the $480,000 press and forcing re-tendering at lower margins.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MCFC's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 10.6% rise in cork bark, resin and freight costs and the 3.0% minimum wage increase will affect MCFC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): If MCFC's $280,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.5 percentage-point rise adds about $1,400 a year of interest — modest against fixed costs of $180,000. It may also raise the cost of financing on eco-housing projects generally, softening order volumes, but the community share element ($200,000) is unaffected by the bank rate and provides a natural hedge. Direct cash impact is small.

Minimum wage increase (3.0% to $11.80): With 29 staff, mainly press operators, cutters and packers, a 3.0% rise adds roughly $19,900 a year (29 × $22,900 average annual wage × 3.0% ≈ $19,900) — meaningful against a $378,000 operating profit, and it lands on top of overtime already needed after 8 press stoppages.

Input-cost inflation (10.6% cork bark, resin and freight): Materials and freight dominate the $9.00 variable cost. If cork bark, resin and freight represent about 55% of variable cost (≈ $4.95), a 10.6% rise adds about $0.52 per unit — roughly $23,600 a year on 45,000 units, compounding with the 5.8% contamination rate that turns premium bark into waste. Unlike wages, this applies at every unit pressed and cannot be renegotiated quickly with Portuguese and Mediterranean suppliers.

Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in cork bark, resin and freight costs will have the greatest impact. It exceeds the wage increase in cash terms, strikes the biggest single cost input of every unit MCFC presses, and compounds with the 5.8% contamination problem to erode the $6.00 contribution at the exact moment MCFC is asking buyers to fund a 7% premium. The wage rise (≈ $19,900) ranks second and the interest-rate rise (≈ $1,400) is containable by fixing the loan. MCFC must renegotiate freight annually, qualify a second bark supplier, tighten dust controls, and only then pass the smallest possible increase into the 7% premium for certified flooring.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to MCFC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MCFC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MCFC with a well-justified judgement that the input-cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
